_about: The nightly's KIT: everything a machine that starts empty needs, beside the checkout, to build the site the laptop builds. Measured and argued in the cloud-move plan of 25 September 2026; read by cloud.py, and held to the build by preflight.

Paths are relative to the working folder, with / between folders. In a glob, * and ? stay inside one folder and ** crosses any number of them. Every entry must match something unless it says optional.

owner says who writes a file. A 'night' file is the nightly's own: the laptop sends it once, with seed-kit, and never over the night's copy after that. A 'laptop' file is made by the laptop's jobs: the night reads it and never sends it back. One writer per file, because two is how the older copy wins.

held is for the one night a term turns over. A New term run's kit-up (--hold) keeps the night's changed files out of kit/, under nights/<run>/kit/, until that run's build has been published and kit-release moves them in: until then the next night takes down the kit as it was, and still refuses the General Court's smaller files. An entry that says "held": false goes to kit/ all the same, because nothing the build or a guard reads comes from it, or because its state travels in state/ whatever happens. Only a night's entry may say it.

state is the handful of small files a night must remember. On a machine they live under archive/, the project's one place for small state (refused.json, census.json); in the bucket they live under state/. backup is the laptop's copy of everything git does not hold, less what it leaves out and why. never is what no command sends anywhere.

kit.what: The day's files, where the nightly installs them: the twelve of snapshot_gencourt.py's fourteen that git does not track. GeneralCodes.txt and BodyStatusCodes.txt arrive with the checkout.

Next session's bill requests, fetch_lsrs.py's lsrs.json: the night takes them since 30 September 2026 (nightly.take_lsrs) and puts the earlier list back whole when a fetch fails. Until then the file was committed to git and fetched by hand.

Each day's copy of those files: what gc_changes.py compares the night's with. Never held: it is the archive of what the General Court served that day, which cannot be asked for again, and neither the build nor the shrink rule reads it.
Past terms' dockets, fetched and dumped: narrate_archive.py, build_manifest.py and extract_chapters.py read them.
The database views the build reads, of the 31 in the dump, and of the six Past* views the one report_check.py reads: the House committee reports of 2016-2024 as the committees filed them.

Each term's current-term views as they stood at its end (db/term/<term>/: Legislation, LegislationText, CandH_Reports and their _columns.json), frozen before the General Court turns the views over to the next term. build_bill_versions.py and senate_hearing_reports.py read them after the current dump, so a past term keeps its versions and Senate hearing reports. Nothing is here until the first freeze, so it may be empty.

A finished term's day files as they were last installed, and their manifest (freeze_term.py --session, frozen/<term>/day/ and frozen/<term>/manifest.json): after the turn build_data.py --frozen-terms builds the term from them every night, and the New term run will not take a new term's files until the term it leaves is frozen as installed. The person sends them with seed-kit on the switch night. Optional: nothing is here until the first freeze, and a required glob that matched nothing would stop every night's kit-down.

The General Court's own text of every past bill's printings, 1989-2024 (fetch_past_db.py; 944 MB). archive_text.py reads it to show 2018's final version where the saved page printed an earlier one, and without it GitHub's build would keep the earlier printing on those 23 bills. It changes only when the laptop dumps the views again.

The General Court's sponsor record for past terms, with the view that guards its join and the manifest that gives both their column order (fetch_past_db.py), and the legislators table that turns its employee numbers into the site's members (fetch_archive_db.py): past_sponsors.py reads all four, and 2023-2024's sponsor lists come from them.

The General Court's docket of past terms as its database's past view holds it (fetch_past_db.py; 94 MB). narrate_archive.py reads it for the bills whose rows the term's own docket file lacks -- SB 340 and SB 499 of 2016, HR 1 to HR 6 of 2017, HB 451 of 2019 and HB 459 of 2021 on 1 October 2026 -- which have no history without it. Optional because the laptop has to send it first: a night that has none builds those bills with no history, and narrate_archive.py says so in its log. It changes only when the laptop dumps the views again.

The study and statutory committees -- their details, meetings and members, and the dump's temporary view of them -- and the dump's manifest, whose StatStudMeetings date the calendar reads. The night's study-committee refresh swaps all four views in whole.
Who sits on each committee, who chairs it, and the members who have left; the night's weekly job refreshes them.

What each committee's own page adds to that list: the clerk, the purpose under the chamber's rules, and the page's roster, from fetch_committee_details.py at a person's word. Its own file because the weekly job swaps committees.json in whole and the listing pages carry neither; build_committees.py joins the two through committee_details.py.
The towns in each Senate district, which the build does not make.
Outputs a build reads before it rewrites them: build_all.CARRIED. Without last night's copy each one changes the site without anything failing.
The archived terms' manifests, one per term, from build_manifest.py --docket.
What the laptop's jobs make and the build reads.

The General Court's list of its calendars and journals, a row a document with the viewer address its own page gives: the Calendar page's picker and the cards' document links are built from it. The night's since 1 October 2026: nightly.take_documents reads the two index pages (fetch_calendar_archive.py --listing) and adds what is new, whole or not at all. Until then it was the laptop's, last discovered on 13 September, and the laptop's seed-kit sent the copy the night started from.

What the General Court's two index pages listed the last time the night read them, in their own words, and when: written with the list above, by the same step. Optional: none exists before the first night that takes the list.

What the laptop's drain has fetched of the documents on the night's list (fetch_calendar_archive.py): the rows whose state it changed, and no others. The list is the night's file, so the drain no longer writes it; the night's listing reads this and marks those documents held in the list the build reads. Optional: none exists until the drain fetches a document the night listed.
The saved bill pages.
The calendars' and journals' text: the .txt beside each PDF, not the PDF.
Times read off the recordings, and where each recording's captions stop: the caption job's answers, not the 20 GB of captions it read them from.

The licensed logo the build lays over the clipart. Private: never in the repository, allowed in the bucket and on the build machine. The header's mark is named by its own path because it has no clipart twin and a glob is satisfied by any one file: a kit sent before build_brand.py drew it is refused on the laptop rather than built without it. brand/licensed/, which it is drawn from, goes to the backup only.

The bought clipart the build copies into the site: the favicon, the tab and app icons, and the clipart lockup and link cards, which assets/licensed/ replaces file for file where it holds one of the same name. Private like the licensed logo and for the same reason: not part of the open-source release, so not in the repository since 1 October 2026. Named one by one, so that a kit missing any single icon is refused rather than built. The header's mark is not among them: it is the artist's drawing, mark.png in assets/licensed/, has no clipart twin, and is named in the entry above. brand/, which build_brand.py draws them from, goes to the backup only.

The one file of last night's site a build reads before it rewrites it: build_pages.py counts the committees with a roster for the home page out of site/committees.json, which build_committees.py writes later in the same build. A build from the kit alone on 25 September differed from the laptop's in this and in two sitemap addresses, of 54,975 files; build_bill_pages.py has since listed those addresses whatever is on disk.

The night's new livestreams: the index rows the committed videos_*.csv do not carry. Their state is archive/livestreams.json, in the state list below. Optional: none exists before the first night that finds a livestream. Never held: the state that says a recording has been seen goes up whatever happens, and a row held back from a night that was never published would be a recording the site never shows.

state.what: A refusal on file: nothing asks the General Court, from either machine, until a person clears it.
The last accepted build's counts and fingerprint, which nightly.py's gates compare with.
The night's verdict, for the morning.
What livestreams.py has seen and waits for, and what it read off recordings the laptop has not yet read. The night writes it; the laptop's --catch-up only reads it.

A hold on the General Court's SQL host: a connection the night could not open (probe_db.py). It expires by itself and lengthens; the night is its one writer, and the web server's refusal record is a different file about a different server.
How far the reader reports have been pulled. A number, never a reader's words.

logs.what: What kit-up sends to logs/<date>/: the night's logs and its what-changed report, written since kit-down.

backup.what: Everything in the working folder that git does not track, except these.

leave_out.why: the repository itself, which GitHub holds, and the assistant's own state
cloud.py's own record of this machine, locks, and files half written
a night's log carries what the report pull printed, which can be a reader's own words; the About page promises those are gone within a week
the built site, remade from the kit and the code every night; --with-site sends it

never.what: Sent by no command: not in the kit, the state or the backup, whatever else matches.
